title: Post-Course Portfolio: Project Management App
descriptionMarkdown:
# Project Management App

## Position in the curriculum
Post-course portfolio expansion: build after finishing the full curriculum through the final capstone, and after the Authentication & User Management System, whose role-based authorization this project extends into a genuinely per-resource permission model (permission depends on team membership, not just a global role).

## Already-proven foundation
This project deliberately reuses the final capstone's own domain shape (tasks with statuses) but adds what the graded core explicitly could not test: teams, per-team membership-based permissions, and an event-driven notification triggered by a state change, applying Chapter 20's Observer pattern to a real, persisted side effect.

## Project scope
Model `Team`, `Membership` (a user, a team, a role such as `OWNER`/`MEMBER`), `Project` (owned by a team), and `Task` (belongs to a project, has a status, an assignee, a due date). Authorization is per-resource and role-dependent: only a team `OWNER` may add or remove members or delete the project; any `MEMBER` may create and update tasks; a task may only be reassigned by its current assignee or an `OWNER`. Implement this as explicit, tested checks in the service layer, not scattered across controllers. When a task's status changes to `DONE` or its due date passes while still open, publish a domain event that a separate notification component listens for and turns into a persisted notification record for the relevant users, keeping the task-update code itself unaware of what listens to it.

## Required evidence
- An authorization test matrix covering every role and every protected operation, including a `MEMBER` attempting an `OWNER`-only action.
- A test confirming a task update publishes exactly the expected event, and a separate test confirming the notification listener correctly turns that event into a stored notification, with the two components tested independently.
- A test for the overdue-task detection using an injected `Clock`, not the system clock.
- A migration history showing the team/membership schema introduced and later extended (for example, adding a new role) as two separate, ordered migrations.
- A short architecture note explaining why the notification listener depends on the task service's published event type rather than the task service depending on the notification component directly.

## Review and completion
A reviewer joins a new member to a team as a `MEMBER`, attempts an `OWNER`-only action as that member (expecting rejection), then performs the same action as the actual `OWNER` (expecting success), and finally advances the system clock past a task's due date and confirms exactly one notification is generated for the right user, not zero and not duplicated on a later, unrelated request.
learningObjectives: Design and test a role-based, per-resource authorization model with more than one permission level
Publish a domain event on a state change and handle it in a component the publisher does not depend on
Detect a time-based condition (an overdue task) deterministically with an injected clock
Keep authorization checks centralized in the service layer rather than duplicated across controllers
Evolve a schema through separate, ordered migrations as requirements grow
